title: Case: a regulated fintech with PII erasure and governed metrics
summary: Classification, tokenization, Snowflake policies, GDPR erasure through every layer and snapshot, audit and lineage, contracts and governed metrics in a regulated lakehouse.

blocks.text: 49.1 Context and requirements

An EU payments fintech with 3 million customers runs a core ledger on Postgres, a KYC service, card-processor settlement files and app events. Its lakehouse follows chapter 47 (CDC into Iceberg, Snowflake on top). Regulation changes the priorities: who can see what, proving it, and removing personal data on request while keeping records that the law requires.

head: Requirement
Source
Design consequence
rows: Erase personal data on valid request within one month
erasure must reach bronze, silver, gold, Kafka and time travel
erasure is not deletion of everything: keep records, remove identity where no legal basis remains
masking, row policies, access history, lineage
governed metrics in a semantic layer
data contracts with versioning and SLAs

blocks.text: Retention obligations and erasure rights conflict. Legal and compliance teams decide which data has which legal basis; the platform's job is to make both outcomes technically possible per field, not to pick one.
49.2 Architecture decision

head: Option
How
Weakness
rows: raw PII in the lake; Snowflake masking and row policies hide it
Spark and anyone with bucket access bypass Snowflake; erasure must rewrite every layer and its history
a PII vault maps values to tokens before bronze; the lake holds tokens
vault becomes critical infrastructure; detokenized use cases need a service
encrypt each subject's fields with a per-subject key; delete the key to erase
key management at scale; encrypted columns cannot be filtered or joined

blocks.title: Architecture decision record
blocks.text:
ADR-044  Personal data in the analytics platform       Status: accepted
Decision: B for direct identifiers (name, email, phone, IBAN, address):
  deterministic tokens, so joins and counts still work. C for free-text
  and documents. Snowflake masking and row policies stay as a second
  layer for quasi-identifiers (birth date, postcode) left in clear.
Why: storage-level controls protect every engine, and erasure becomes
  'delete from the vault' plus a bounded clean-up of quasi-identifiers.
Consequences: vault owned by the security platform team with 99.9%
  SLA; detokenization only through an audited service.

blocks.text: 49.4 Classification and data model

head: Class
Examples
Handling
rows: tokenized before bronze; detokenize via service
clear in silver; masked or generalized in gold
row access by entity and country
not ingested, or encrypted per subject

blocks.text: Classification is stored as tags in the catalog and in Snowflake, set by the contract, not guessed downstream. Gold facts reference `customer_token`; `dim_customer` holds the token, a generalized age band and region, never names. Deterministic tokens keep joins working; a deleted vault entry leaves an orphan token that no longer resolves to a person.

An orphan token is not automatic anonymisation. Birth date, postcode and a rare transaction pattern can still single someone out. Erasure must also null or generalize quasi-identifiers for that token.
49.5 Controls with code

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: tag-based masking and row access

blocks.text: Tag-based masking means a newly tagged column is protected without anyone writing a policy for it. Policy support on Iceberg tables, especially externally managed ones, should be checked in the current documentation (chapter 28). Remember these policies govern Snowflake queries only; files read by Spark rely on tokenization and bucket policy (chapter 34).

blocks.title: Snowflake SQL: who read customer data in 30 days
blocks.text:
SELECT ah.query_start_time, ah.user_name,
       obj.value:objectName::STRING AS object_name
FROM snowflake.account_usage.access_history ah,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => ah.base_objects_accessed) obj
WHERE obj.value:objectName::STRING ILIKE '%DIM_CUSTOMER'
  AND ah.query_start_time > DATEADD(day, -30, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP());

Access history answers *who read what*; OpenLineage events from Spark, dbt and the orchestrator answer *where it came from* (chapter 33). Auditors usually ask for both, plus evidence that policies were in place at the time.

blocks.text: 49.6 Erasure across layers and time
Erasure is a workflow, not a query. A request is validated by the compliance team, the vault deletes the mapping, and a pipeline cleans every copy, then records evidence.

head: Copy
Mechanism
Physically gone after
rows: `expire_snapshots` older than 7 days, then orphan removal
Time Travel retention, then Fail-safe (7 days)
retention plus Fail-safe; check current docs

blocks.text: With merge-on-read, a `DELETE` only writes a delete file; the old data file still contains the row until compaction rewrites it and snapshot expiry removes the old file (chapters 23, 25). Time-travel retention is therefore a privacy setting: it must be shorter than the erasure deadline minus processing time.

Regulatory reports need reproducibility, which tempts teams to tag Iceberg snapshots and keep them for years. Because the lake holds tokens, a retained snapshot is safe: erasure still works by deleting the vault entry.
49.7 Governed metrics, SLAs and failure modes

Metrics such as *net interchange revenue*, *fraud loss rate* and *active customers* are defined once in the semantic layer (chapter 35), each with an owning team, a version and a change review. Regulatory reports query a pinned metric version against a recorded snapshot, so a rerun months later gives the same number.

items: A producer team renames a field in a minor release; the contract check in CI blocks it and the team ships a major version instead.

The analytics team, using a role with `PII_READER`, copies `dim_customer` into a sandbox with `CREATE TABLE AS`; the copy holds clear values and, unless tag propagation is configured (check current docs), no tags. Restrict create rights for PII roles and scan for untagged columns matching PII patterns.
Snapshot expiry is paused during an incident and never resumed; erasure evidence becomes false. Alert on snapshot age per table.
The vault is down and ingestion blocks; buffer in Kafka rather than bypass tokenization.

blocks.title: Erasure audit
blocks.text: An auditor picks 20 erasure requests from last quarter and asks for proof.
items: Vault deletion log with request id and timestamp.
Pipeline run ids for the quasi-identifier clean-up and the following compaction.
Snapshot expiry logs showing no snapshot older than the cut-off.
A query showing the token no longer resolves and quasi-identifiers are null.

blocks.title: Right of access
blocks.text: Customers can also request a copy of all data held about them within one month. Design the process across vault, lake, Snowflake and the semantic layer, keeping it auditable and without giving analysts general access to clear-text PII.
hints: Which system knows every place a token appears?
Who runs the detokenization, and how is it logged?
How do you avoid the export becoming a new uncontrolled copy?

items: Classify at the contract, store classification as tags, and let tags drive masking.
Tokenize direct identifiers before bronze so every engine, not only Snowflake, is protected.
Erasure reaches Kafka, every Iceberg layer, old snapshots and warehouse time travel; retention settings are privacy settings.
Orphaned tokens are not anonymisation; clean quasi-identifiers too.
Access history plus lineage plus policy history is the audit evidence.
Governed, versioned metrics make regulatory numbers reproducible.

blocks.q: Why is relying only on Snowflake masking policies insufficient here?
options: Masking policies do not work on views
Engines reading the Iceberg files directly bypass Snowflake policies
Masking is too slow for large tables
blocks.explain: Policies apply to queries through Snowflake. Spark or anyone with file access sees raw values, which is why the lake holds tokens.

blocks.q: After `DELETE FROM silver.customers WHERE ...` on a merge-on-read Iceberg table, when is the row physically gone?
options: Immediately, because DELETE rewrites the files
Only when the table is dropped
After compaction rewrites the data file and the old snapshots are expired and their files removed
blocks.explain: Merge-on-read writes a delete file; old data files remain referenced by earlier snapshots until rewrite plus expiry.

blocks.q: A vault entry is deleted, leaving orphan tokens in gold. What else is needed?
options: Clean or generalize quasi-identifiers linked to the token
Drop the gold tables and rebuild them
blocks.explain: Quasi-identifiers can still single a person out. Rebuilding everything is unnecessary.

blocks.q: Why do regulatory reports query a pinned metric version and a recorded snapshot?
options: So a rerun months later reproduces the submitted number
Snowflake requires it for Iceberg tables
blocks.explain: Definitions and data change; pinning both makes the number reproducible.
